title: Jeremiah 34:1–7
context: The narrator sets the scene: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and his armies are fighting against Jerusalem and its cities, and only Lachish and Azekah remain among Judah’s fortified cities (34:1, 34:7). The LORD sends Jeremiah to King Zedekiah with a twofold word. The city will be given to the king of Babylon and burned, and Zedekiah will not escape but will see the king of Babylon eye to eye and go to Babylon (34:2–3). Yet the LORD also says, “You won’t die by the sword. You will die in peace,” with burnings and lament as for the former kings (34:4–5). Jeremiah delivers these words to Zedekiah (34:6). Later chapters report that Zedekiah was captured, saw his sons killed at Riblah, was blinded, and was taken to Babylon in fetters (39:5–7; 52:9–11; 2 Kings 25:6–7), and 52:11 adds that he was kept in prison until his death. How the promise of dying “in peace” relates to that fate is not explained in the text, and this page names the parallels without harmonizing them. Both traditions read the unit as shared ground: the LORD’s word to the king is sure, and it comes in a time of real siege and danger.

verses.text: The word which came to Jeremiah from the LORD, when Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, with all his army, all the kingdoms of the earth that were under his dominion, and all the peoples, were fighting against Jerusalem and against all its cities, saying:
verses.arminianNotes: The word comes while Nebuchadnezzar and all his armies fight against Jerusalem. Arminian readers note the setting of extreme danger. The LORD speaks into a real historical crisis, and the king’s choices are made under the pressure of siege.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that the LORD’s word comes in the midst of the nations’ armies, which he governs. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as placing the prophetic word in a concrete historical moment, and neither treats the setting as merely symbolic.

verses.text: “The LORD, the God of Israel, says, ‘Go, and speak to Zedekiah king of Judah, and tell him, the LORD says, “Behold, I will give this city into the hand of the king of Babylon and he will burn it with fire.
verses.arminianNotes: “Behold, I will give this city into the hand of the king of Babylon.” Arminian readers note that the LORD tells the king plainly what is coming. The word is not hidden but declared, giving Zedekiah a clear warning.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD announcing his purpose in judgment on the city. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a sure word of judgment, spoken openly to the king, and both see the burning of the city as a consequence of long covenant unfaithfulness.

verses.text: You won’t escape out of his hand, but will surely be taken and delivered into his hand. Your eyes will see the eyes of the king of Babylon, and he will speak with you mouth to mouth. You will go to Babylon.” ’
verses.arminianNotes: Zedekiah will not escape; he will see the king of Babylon “mouth to mouth” and go to Babylon. Arminian readers note the personal nature of the warning. The king himself will face the conqueror, as later chapters report (39:5–7).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the certainty of the word and its later fulfillment (compare 52:9–11 and 2 Kings 25:6–7). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a personal word to the king that later chapters show coming to pass.

verses.text: “Yet hear the LORD’s word, O Zedekiah king of Judah. The LORD says concerning you, ‘You won’t die by the sword.
verses.arminianNotes: “Yet hear the LORD’s word… You won’t die by the sword.” Arminian readers note the turn to a word of mitigation. Even within judgment, the LORD speaks a word that limits what will happen to Zedekiah himself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the word of mercy within judgment. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a real promise to the king, and both read it alongside the later accounts of his fate (39:6–7; 52:10–11) without forcing a single explanation.

verses.text: You will die in peace; and with the burnings of your fathers, the former kings who were before you, so they will make a burning for you. They will lament you, saying, “Ah Lord!” for I have spoken the word,’ says the LORD.”
verses.arminianNotes: “You will die in peace,” with burnings and lament as for former kings. Arminian readers note that the text does not explain how this relates to Zedekiah’s later blinding and imprisonment (52:11). They hold the question openly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise acknowledge that the text leaves the relation unexplained and do not force a harmony. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a word of mercy to the king and name the later accounts (39:5–7; 52:9–11; 2 Kings 25:6–7) plainly.

verses.text: Then Jeremiah the prophet spoke all these words to Zedekiah king of Judah in Jerusalem,
verses.arminianNotes: “Then Jeremiah the prophet spoke all these words to Zedekiah.” Arminian readers note the prophet’s faithfulness. Jeremiah delivers both the hard word and the word of mercy, without softening either, to a king who holds power over him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Jeremiah’s obedience in carrying the word to the king. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as an example of faithful prophetic witness, speaking the whole message entrusted to the messenger.

verses.text: when the king of Babylon’s army was fighting against Jerusalem and against all the cities of Judah that were left, against Lachish and against Azekah; for these alone remained of the cities of Judah as fortified cities.
verses.arminianNotes: Only Lachish and Azekah remain among Judah’s fortified cities. Arminian readers note how close the end is. The detail shows the shrinking of Judah’s defenses and the seriousness of the moment in which the king must hear the word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the narrowing circle of the siege. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as historical setting, and neither builds conclusions beyond the narrator’s note that these alone remained as fortified cities.
